account:
Today I have kept my morning office hours and arrived at the mill for the ten o'clock grain inspection, though I have not yet found the miller. This morning the secretary reported no audiences or new public business. Our search found no council letters or correspondence: the appointments chest held the two schedule books, and the treasury held 128 emeralds, with no accounts or letters. That absence is curious but does not establish wrongdoing.

There are signs of arrangements being made without my full knowledge. The secretary previously told me that the innkeeper collected bread from the baker and said the inn owes forty-four emeralds, payable after the jubilee. The secretary did not establish who ordered the bread or its purpose. Freight apparently asked that their arrangements remain private until today at eighteen. My appointment addendum reserves precisely eighteen for the builder's great hall lighting inspection, and the innkeeper has arranged to collect me at my office at seventeen forty-five. These overlapping details make me suspect preparations for a jubilee gathering, perhaps a surprise celebration with bread and lighting in the great hall. That is a hypothesis, not something I have witnessed or had confirmed.

The neighbour has confirmed our usual fifteen o'clock tea at the east-bank cottage; the addendum says no special preparations are needed. I do not know whether that visit is connected with anything else. Near the mill, Townsfolk 21 has twice said 'bridge or port change at bakery.' I do not understand the phrase or know whether it concerns an actual change. I also heard the baker shouting earlier but could not make out the words. I should not treat either as evidence of a particular plan. For now I intend to keep my appointments, inspect the grain if the miller can be found, and learn more through ordinary conversation rather than assume a secret scheme.
